usage: The everyday default: 잔 covers any served drink — coffee, tea, water, beer, soju.
Bar shorthand for another round; you'll hear this constantly while drinking together.
Written as ONE word, this is a verb meaning 'go have a (casual) drink', not literally one glass.
Spacing matters: number + space + 잔 (세 잔), never 세잔.
examples: 물 한 잔 주세요.
One glass of water, please.
Simplest form: [noun] + [native number] + 잔. The counter comes AFTER the number, before the verb.
저는 하루에 커피를 세 잔씩 마셔요.
I drink three cups of coffee each day.
Note 씩 ('each/per') after the counter — '세 잔씩' = three cups apiece per day, a natural habit phrase.
딱 한 잔만 더 하고 갈게요.
I'll have just one more drink and then go.
Real bar line: 딱...만 = 'just exactly one', and 한 잔 하다 here means 'have a drink', not eat.
nuance: 잔 is the counter for a serving of liquid held in a cup or glass — it counts the POURED drink, not the container itself. Its near-rivals are 병 (a whole bottle) and 컵 (the physical cup as an object), and the dividing line is what you're measuring: 맥주 한 병 is a full bottle, 맥주 한 잔 is one glass poured from it. The hanja is 盞 ('small cup'), though it feels fully native in use and always takes native-Korean numbers (한, 두, 세 잔), never Sino-Korean 일/이. Watch two traps: 한잔하다 written together is a VERB ('go for a drink') and is idiomatic, so don't read it as a literal count; and English 'a cup of coffee' tempts learners to reach for 컵, but the natural measure word for the drink itself is 잔.

mistakes: Saying 일 잔, 이 잔 with Sino-Korean numbers. Counters of servings take native numbers: 한 잔, 두 잔, 세 잔.
Using 잔 to count bottles. A sealed/whole bottle is 병 (맥주 두 병); 잔 is only the glass poured out.
Writing the drink-verb as two words '한 잔 하다' when you mean the idiom 'grab a drink' — the set verb is 한잔하다, one word.

usage: 켤레 counts things worn as a matching two-of-a-kind: shoes, socks, gloves.
Native numbers only: 한, 두, 세 켤레 — never 일 켤레.
The go-to question form when buying footwear or socks.
Gloves arrive as a set of two, so 켤레, not 개.
examples: 운동화 한 켤레 사고 싶어요.
I want to buy a pair of sneakers.
Basic shape: [item] + 한 켤레. One 켤레 = the whole pair, both shoes together.
양말 세 켤레에 오천 원이에요.
Three pairs of socks are 5,000 won.
Market pricing pattern: [quantity]에 [price]. 세 켤레에 = 'for three pairs'.
등산하려고 두꺼운 양말 두 켤레를 챙겼어요.
I packed two pairs of thick socks to go hiking.
두 켤레를 marks the object; -려고 ('in order to') gives the purpose.
nuance: 켤레 is the dedicated counter for items that come and are worn as a matched pair — shoes, sneakers, boots, socks, and gloves. The key conceptual point is that ONE 켤레 already means BOTH pieces together (the left and the right), so it functions like English 'a pair'; its near-synonym 짝, by contrast, isolates a SINGLE one of the two, as in 양말 한 짝 ('one sock' — implying its partner is missing). 켤레 is a native Korean word (no hanja) and always pairs with native numbers (한, 두, 세 켤레). The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 개 because English counts 'a pair of shoes' as one set of objects — but footwear and hand/foot-wear that come in twos must take 켤레; another is calling a single lost shoe 한 켤레, when one of the pair is 한 짝.

mistakes: Counting shoes with 개. 개 is the all-purpose counter for generic objects; matched footwear takes 켤레 (신발 한 켤레).
Saying 두 켤레 for one pair. A single pair (both shoes) is 한 켤레; 두 켤레 means two complete pairs.
Calling one sock 한 켤레. A lone single of the pair is 한 짝 (양말 한 짝); 켤레 always means both.

usage: 벌 counts a complete garment or coordinated set: a suit, a dress, pajamas, hanbok.
A suit (jacket + trousers) counts as a single 벌 — one set.
Asks the count of garments or sets.
Native numbers go before 벌: 한, 두, 세 벌.
examples: 잠옷 한 벌 사려고 해요.
I'm planning to buy a set of pajamas.
Simple: [clothing] + 한 벌. Pajamas (top + bottom) are one 벌, not two.
출근용 정장을 한 벌 새로 맞췄어요.
I had a new work suit custom-made.
맞추다 = 'have tailor-made'; 출근용 = 'for commuting/work'. The whole suit = 한 벌.
이번 여행에는 갈아입을 옷을 세 벌만 챙겼어요.
For this trip I packed only three changes of clothes.
세 벌만 = 'just three sets'; 갈아입다 = 'to change clothes'.
nuance: 벌 counts clothing as a COMPLETE garment or a coordinated outfit, so a suit, dress, hanbok, or pajama set is 한 벌 even though it physically has several pieces — the counter measures the whole worn unit, not the parts. Its near-synonyms split by what they measure: 벌 is the full set, while 장 counts a single flat piece (티셔츠 한 장 — one tee) and 개 is the casual generic count. 벌 is native Korean (no hanja) and takes native numbers. The biggest English-speaker trap is logic-counting the pieces: a two-piece suit feels like 'two items', but the matching set is 한 벌, not 두 벌. A second trap is genre confusion — clothes are 벌, but the shoes that complete the look are 켤레, so don't say 신발 한 벌.

mistakes: Counting a two-piece suit as 두 벌. The jacket-and-trousers set together is 한 벌 (one set).
Using 벌 for shoes. Footwear takes 켤레 (신발 한 켤레); clothing takes 벌.
Counting a single T-shirt as 한 벌 in casual speech. A flat single top is more naturally 티셔츠 한 장 or 한 개; 벌 leans toward full sets.

usage: 권 counts bound things: books, notebooks, magazines, comic volumes.
Native numbers go before 권: 한, 두, 세 권.
The standard quantity question for anything bound.
Each volume of a series is counted separately as a 권.
examples: 공책 한 권 주세요.
One notebook, please.
Basic: [bound item] + 한 권. Notebooks count with 권 just like books.
한 달에 책을 두 권 정도 읽어요.
I read about two books a month.
두 권 정도 = 'about two'; 정도 turns an exact count into an estimate.
도서관에서 빌린 책 세 권을 오늘 반납해야 해요.
I have to return the three library books I borrowed today.
세 권을 marks the books as the object; 반납하다 = 'to return (borrowed items)'.
nuance: 권 is the counter for anything BOUND into a spine — novels, textbooks, notebooks, magazines, and each separate volume of a multi-volume series. Its critical contrast is with 장, which counts a single loose SHEET: 종이 한 장 is one sheet of paper, but the whole bound book made of many sheets is 책 한 권. The hanja is 卷, originally 'a scroll/roll', which is why it now measures a complete bound work. It always takes native-Korean numbers and is among the most frequent counters when you talk about reading or studying. The classic English-speaker pitfall is defaulting to the all-purpose 개 ('책 두 개') because English just says 'two books' — but printed/bound works specifically take 권; a related slip is using 권 for a single page, when one page is 한 장.

mistakes: Using 개 for books. 개 is for generic objects; bound books and volumes specifically take 권 (책 한 권).
Counting loose pages with 권. A single sheet/page is 장 (종이 한 장); the whole book is 권.
Counting a multi-volume set as 한 권 when you mean the whole series. Each volume is its own 권 (전 5권 = '5 volumes total').

usage: 장 counts flat, thin things: paper, tickets, photos, cards, banknotes.
Movie, concert, and transport tickets are counted with 장.
The quantity question for sheets, tickets, or photos.
Thin flat foods (김, a cheese slice) also use 장.
examples: 영화표 두 장 주세요.
Two movie tickets, please.
Counter-window basic: [ticket] + 두 장 + 주세요. Tickets are flat, so 장.
복사 용지 열 장만 주시겠어요?
Could you give me just ten sheets of copy paper?
열 장만 = 'just ten sheets'; 만 caps the amount, and -시겠어요 makes it polite.
가족사진을 한 장 인화하려고 사진관에 갔어요.
I went to a photo studio to print one family photo.
한 장 counts the photo; 인화하다 = 'to develop/print a photograph'.
nuance: 장 counts flat, thin items — sheets of paper, tickets, photographs, banknotes, stickers, postcards, and even thin foods like a sheet of dried seaweed (김) or a slice of cheese. Its sharpest contrast is with 권: 장 is the single loose SHEET, whereas many sheets bound together become 책 한 권 (a book). The hanja is 張, meaning 'to stretch/spread out flat', which captures exactly the flatness it measures. It always takes native numbers and is one of the most-used counters in daily errands — at ticket counters, copy machines, and photo booths. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 개 (a generic count) for tickets and photos because English says 'two tickets'; the natural, expected counter is 장. A second trap is using 장 for a whole magazine or book, which is 권, since those are bound, not loose.

Mixing up 장 with 잔 (a glass of drink). They are different words and counters — 종이 한 장 vs 커피 한 잔.

usage: 대 counts vehicles and machines: cars, bikes, phones, computers, ACs.
Native numbers go before 대: 한, 두, 세 대.
The quantity question for vehicles or appliances.
Home appliances and electronics count with 대.
examples: 우리 집에 차가 한 대 있어요.
There's one car in our household.
Basic existence: [thing]이/가 한 대 있어요. 차가 한 대 있어요 = 'have one car'.
사무실에 컴퓨터가 다섯 대나 있어요.
There are as many as five computers in the office.
다섯 대나 — the 나 after the counter adds the surprised nuance 'as many as'.
오래된 에어컨을 한 대 더 설치하기로 했어요.
We decided to install one more old air conditioner.
한 대 더 = 'one more unit'; -기로 하다 = 'decide to'. Appliances take 대.
nuance: 대 is the all-purpose counter for machines and vehicles — cars, motorcycles, bicycles, computers, phones, cameras, TVs, washing machines, and air conditioners — basically anything mechanical or electronic, so a resident reaches for it constantly when talking about appliances. The hanja is 臺 ('platform/stand'), historically the base a machine sat on, which is why it measures equipment. It contrasts with 채 (whole buildings) and 명 (people): the vehicle is 대, the people riding inside it are 명. It always takes native-Korean numbers. The main English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the generic 개 ('차 두 개') because English just says 'two cars'; machines and vehicles specifically take 대. A subtler trap is counting passengers with 대 — only the machine is 대, while the humans in it are counted with 명.

Counting the people riding in a vehicle with 대. People are 명 (세 명); only the vehicle itself is 대.
Saying 일 대, 이 대 with Sino-Korean numbers. Use native numbers: 한 대, 두 대, 세 대.

usage: 채 counts whole houses and freestanding buildings.
Native numbers go before 채: 한, 두, 세 채.
The quantity question for houses or buildings.
채 is used when counting an apartment unit as an owned property.
examples: 우리 동네에 집이 한 채 비어 있어요.
There's one empty house in our neighborhood.
Basic: [building]이/가 한 채. 비어 있다 = 'be (standing) empty'.
할머니는 시골에 집을 한 채 가지고 계세요.
My grandmother owns a house in the countryside.
한 채 counts the house; 계세요 is the honorific of 있다 ('has/owns'), respecting grandmother.
이 일대에 새 아파트가 두 채나 들어섰어요.
As many as two new apartment buildings went up in this area.
두 채나 — 나 stresses the surprising number; 들어서다 = '(a building) goes up/is established'.
nuance: 채 counts entire dwellings and sizeable standalone buildings — houses, traditional homes (한옥), and apartment buildings or units treated as whole properties — and it always refers to the STRUCTURE as a complete unit, not the rooms inside. Its near-synonym 동 is the counter used for numbered apartment BLOCKS in a complex (101동), while 채 counts the home as one property; rooms within, meanwhile, are 개 (방 두 개). 채 is a native Korean word (no hanja) and takes native numbers. You meet it most in real-estate talk and neighborhood descriptions. The English-speaker pitfall is the generic 개 ('집 두 개') because English says 'two houses'; whole buildings specifically take 채. Another trap is using 대 (the machine counter) for a building by analogy — buildings are never 대.

mistakes: Counting rooms inside a home with 채. Individual rooms are 개 (방 한 개); the whole house/building is 채.
Using 대 for a building. 대 is for machines and vehicles; a house or building takes 채.
Defaulting to 개 for houses. A whole dwelling takes 채 (집 한 채), not the generic 개.

english: counter for flowers and clustered fruit
usage: 송이 counts a single blossom or a naturally clustered bunch.
Native numbers go before 송이: 한, 두, 세 송이.
Fruit that grows in clusters (grapes, bananas) is counted with 송이.
The quantity question for flowers or grape bunches.
examples: 장미 한 송이만 주세요.
Just one rose, please.
Flower-shop basic: [flower] + 한 송이. 만 = 'just', softening to a single bloom.
포도 한 송이에 만 원이에요.
One bunch of grapes is 10,000 won.
송이 counts the grape cluster; [quantity]에 [price] is fruit-stand pricing.
졸업식 날 여자친구에게 꽃을 한 송이 건넸어요.
On graduation day I handed my girlfriend a single flower.
한 송이 counts the bloom; 건네다 = 'to hand over', and 에게 = 'to (a person)'.
nuance: 송이 counts a single blossom on its stem or a naturally formed cluster of produce — one rose, one tulip, a bunch of grapes, a hand of bananas. Its essential contrast is with 다발: 송이 is ONE separate bloom or cluster, whereas 다발 is a tied BUNDLE of many (꽃 한 다발 = a bouquet, 꽃 한 송이 = a single flower). 송이 is native Korean (no hanja) and takes native numbers. It surfaces whenever you buy flowers or cluster-fruit. The English-speaker pitfall is the generic 개 ('장미 두 개') because English says 'two roses'; a flower naturally takes 송이. A subtler trap is calling a wrapped bouquet 한 송이 — a gift bouquet is 한 다발, while 송이 stays reserved for each individual stem or cluster.

Calling a wrapped bouquet 한 송이. A bound bouquet is 한 다발; 송이 is one individual flower or cluster.
Counting loose individual grapes with 송이. The whole hanging cluster is 한 송이; single berries are 알 (포도 한 알).

english: counter for rows, lines, and strips (e.g. gimbap)
usage: 줄 counts long line-shaped things: a gimbap roll, a row, a line of text.
Native numbers go before 줄: 한, 두, 세 줄.
to line up in a single row
한 줄로 + 서다 is a fixed phrase for forming one queue.
The quantity question for lines of text or rows.
examples: 김밥 한 줄 주세요.
One roll of gimbap, please.
Snack-shop basic: 김밥 + 한 줄. The whole uncut roll is 한 줄, not the slices.
여기 한 줄로 서 주세요.
Please line up in a single line here.
한 줄로 = 'into one line'; the 로 marks the resulting arrangement. Common queue instruction.
이 긴 글을 두 줄로 짧게 요약해 봤어요.
I summarized this long text into two short lines.
두 줄로 = 'into two lines'; 줄 counts written lines as well as physical rows.
nuance: 줄 counts things stretched out in a long line — a roll of gimbap (a long tube of rice and fillings), a row of seats, a queue of people, and lines of written text. As a plain noun 줄 also means 'a line/string/rope', and the counter inherits that 'long linear thing' image. Its everyday rivals split by shape: 줄 is the whole long line, but once gimbap is sliced, each round piece becomes 개 (김밥 한 개 = one slice). 줄 is native Korean (no hanja) and takes native numbers; note the set phrase 한 줄로 서다 ('stand in a single line'), heard constantly in queues. The English-speaker pitfall is counting cut gimbap pieces with 줄 — the uncut roll is 한 줄, individual slices are 개; another is using 개 for a row or queue when the natural counter is 줄.

Using 개 for a queue or a row. A line of people or a row is 줄 (한 줄), not the generic 개.
Forgetting the 로 in the line-up phrase. The natural instruction is 한 줄로 서다 ('line up into one row'), with 로.

usage: 마리 counts every kind of animal: pets, fish, birds, insects, livestock.
Native numbers go before 마리: 한, 두, 세 마리.
The quantity question for any creature.
A whole (cooked) chicken is counted with 마리 too.
examples: 강아지 한 마리 키우고 싶어요.
I want to raise one puppy.
Basic: [animal] + 한 마리. 키우다 = 'to raise/keep (a pet)'.
우리 집 어항에는 금붕어가 세 마리 있어요.
There are three goldfish in our fish tank.
세 마리 counts the fish; even tiny creatures take 마리, regardless of size.
배고픈데 치킨 한 마리 시켜 먹을까요?
I'm hungry — shall we order a whole chicken?
한 마리 counts the chicken; 시켜 먹다 = 'order in and eat'. Classic fried-chicken line.
nuance: 마리 is the universal counter for animals — dogs, cats, fish, birds, insects, livestock, and even a whole cooked chicken or fish on the table. Crucially it is size-independent: the same word counts an ant (개미 한 마리) and an elephant (코끼리 한 마리). 마리 is native Korean (no hanja) and takes native numbers. Its single most important contrast is with 명, the counter for PEOPLE: animals are 마리, humans are 명, and crossing that line matters socially. 마리 is also distinct from 분, the honorific people-counter. The big English-speaker pitfall is using 마리 for people because English says 'two' for both — but calling a person 한 마리 is insulting or mocking (treating them like an animal); always use 명 (or honorific 분) for humans. A second slip is the generic 개 for animals, which sounds wrong — creatures take 마리.

Saying 일 마리, 이 마리 with Sino-Korean numbers. Use native numbers: 한 마리, 두 마리, 세 마리.

usage: 끼 counts meal OCCASIONS: breakfast, lunch, dinner as sittings.
Native numbers go before 끼: 한, 두, 세 끼.
The quantity question for meal sittings.
to make do with a quick meal
한 끼 + 때우다 is a set phrase for grabbing a quick bite to get by.
examples: 저는 하루에 두 끼 먹어요.
I eat two meals a day.
Basic habit: 하루에 [number] 끼 먹다. 끼 counts the sittings, not the dishes.
오늘 너무 바빠서 한 끼밖에 못 먹었어요.
I was so busy today I only ate one meal.
한 끼밖에 + 못 — 밖에 ('only') REQUIRES a negative verb, here 못 먹었어요.
다이어트 중이라 저녁 한 끼는 가볍게 먹으려고 해요.
I'm dieting, so I try to eat one light dinner.
한 끼는 topic-marks the meal; -려고 하다 = 'try/intend to'. 중이라 = 'because I'm in the middle of'.
nuance: 끼 counts meal OCCASIONS — one sitting of breakfast, lunch, or dinner is 한 끼 — so it measures the eating event, not the individual dishes on the table. This is its key contrast with 그릇 (a bowl/serving of food) and 개 (a single dish): 밥 한 끼 is one whole meal, while 밥 한 그릇 is one bowl of rice within it. 끼 is native Korean (no hanja) and takes native numbers. It's the natural way to talk about eating habits, skipping meals, and meal plans (하루 세 끼). Note the set phrase 한 끼 때우다 ('grab a quick bite to get by'). The English-speaker pitfall is using 끼 to count plates or dishes because English loosely says 'a meal' for food generally — but 끼 is the whole sitting; a single dish is 개 or 그릇. A second slip is Sino-Korean numbers (일 끼), when only native 한 끼, 두 끼 work.

usage: 군데 counts locations or spots: shops, sites, even sore spots on the body.
Native numbers go before 군데: 한, 두, 세 군데.
Extremely common: 몇 군데 = 'how many spots/places'.
여러 군데 = 'in several spots/places', for scattered locations or pains.
examples: 여기 근처에 카페가 몇 군데 있어요?
How many cafés are there near here?
Basic: [place] + 몇 군데. 군데 counts the locations being asked about.
병원을 세 군데나 다녀 봤어요.
I even went to as many as three different hospitals.
세 군데나 — the 나 stresses 'as many as three'; 다니다 = 'go around/attend (repeatedly)'.
넘어져서 몸이 여러 군데 아파요.
I fell, so I ache in several spots on my body.
여러 군데 = 'in several places'; 군데 counts sore spots too, not just shops.
nuance: 군데 counts locations or spots — shops you visited, apartments you toured, websites you checked, or places on the body that hurt — and it works equally for distinct establishments and for scattered points. Its near-synonym is 곳, which also means 'place', but 곳 is a fuller noun ('a place') and can stand alone or sound slightly more formal/written, whereas 군데 is specifically the conversational COUNTER you attach to a number (세 군데, 여러 군데). 군데 is native Korean (no hanja) and takes native numbers. It pairs constantly with 몇 군데 ('how many places') and 여러 군데 ('several places'). The English-speaker pitfall is the generic 개 for places because English says 'three places'; locations naturally take 군데 (or 곳). A separate, embarrassing trap is mixing 군데 (a spot) with the look-alike 군대 ('the military/army') — wholly different words.
